queued.critic_reason: claims are plausible and testable given available data and mechanism
queued.data_source: IMF International Financial Statistics and central bank published data
queued.evidence: IMF IFS data; no lab test; prior version dropped for lack of power
queued.mechanism: Central bank gold purchases create forced long physical demand and subsequent delivery or lease flows that affect gold futures.
queued.needs_short_or_leverage: no short; leverage optional for sizing
queued.rule: When net central bank gold purchases exceed 100 tonnes in a quarter, go long gold futures; exit after six months or when net purchases turn negative.
queued.title: Central Bank Gold Purchases and Physical Delivery Follow-Through
queued.why: at its claimed strength it expects t 4.472 against 3.0 (passes 93% of the time); the claim must be verified at its source before it is built

queued.critic_reason: New family on an untested universe (us-treasury-daily, 0 tests) with a coherent risk-premium mechanism (inflation-risk term premium compressing as yields revert). The rule is fully causal (rolling 252-day percentile, 50-day SMA exit), H.15 yields are point-in-time and public, and Treasury CFDs exist. At the claimed net Sharpe of 1.2 over 10 fresh years, t is about 3.8 against a bar of 3.0, and two instruments traded as one book double the data; costs on liquid bond CFDs are small. Whether the edge survives is for the statistics.
queued.data_source: US Treasury daily yield data (Federal Reserve H.15) and corresponding CFD price data
queued.mechanism: Investors demand a premium for holding nominal bonds during periods of high macroeconomic uncertainty or inflation volatility. When inflation expectations spike, the required term premium increases, causing nominal bond yields to rise and bond prices to fall. Patient capital willing to bear inflation risk buys these bonds at rich yields, capturing the premium as expectations stabilize and yields revert. This persists because inflation risk is systematic and cannot be diversified away by most investors, who face constraints on holding long-duration assets during high inflation.
queued.rule: At the daily close, compute the 10-year Treasury yield. If the current yield is in the top 10% of the rolling 252-day window, enter a long position in the 10-year Treasury CFD. Hold the position until the yield falls below its 50-day simple moving average, at which point exit to cash. If the yield is not in the top 10% at the close, remain in cash. This rule spans 2 instruments (the 10-year and 30-year Treasury CFDs) traded as one book.
queued.title: Treasury Inflation Expectations Risk Premium
queued.why: at its claimed strength it expects t 3.795 against 3.0 (passes 79% of the time); the claim must be verified at its source before it is built
queued.why_new: This is the first proposal in the risk premium class on the completely untested us-treasury-daily universe. While the general bond risk premium is well-documented in academic literature, it has not been tested as a daily CFD trading rule in a swap-free account, and the specific mechanism of inflation risk premium compression captured via yield-percentile mean reversion is new to this lab's registry.

queued.critic_reason: The US sector-rotation lead-lag family was dropped for lack of power ONLY and its entry explicitly opens the door to the same mechanism on more independent instruments traded as one book. This version does exactly that with international sector ETFs, so it is a new test rather than a repeat. The spillover/rebalancing mechanism is a real cross-asset linkage, Yahoo daily ETF prices are obtainable, and the rule (signal at the close, trade at the next open) can be run without look-ahead. Whether a daily-rebalanced 20-position book can keep a 1.2 net Sharpe after ETF spreads is a cost and power question for the statistics, not a ground for rejection here.
queued.data_source: Yahoo Finance daily ETF price data
queued.mechanism: When US investors rotate into or out of a sector, the resulting flows spill over to international markets due to global portfolio rebalancing and correlated trading, causing the same sector in other countries to move in the same direction with a delay. This cross-asset linkage creates a predictable lead-lag pattern.
queued.rule: At each day's close, compute the daily return for each US sector ETF. For each international sector ETF, if the corresponding US sector ETF's return on that day is in the top half of all US sectors, go long the international sector ETF at the next open; if in the bottom half, go short. Hold for one trading day (close to close). Rebalance daily. Equal weight per position, with a maximum of 10 positions long and 10 short.
queued.title: International sector rotation lead-lag among equity ETFs
queued.why: at its claimed strength it expects t 3.795 against 3.0 (passes 79% of the time); the claim must be verified at its source before it is built
queued.why_new: The original sector rotation lead-lag was tested on US ETFs only and dropped for lack of power (t < 3.0). This version uses international ETFs as one book, multiplying the number of independent observations and thus increasing statistical power to detect the effect.

queued.critic_reason: The volatility-managed country equity ETF family was dropped for lack of power ONLY, with the stated remedy being more years or about two independent instruments traded as one book. Thirty country ETFs over twelve years is a breadth version that answers that lack, so it is not a repeat of a closed family. The rule is a cross-sectional volatility sort rather than the dynamic scaling described in the mechanism paragraph, and the mechanism text mislabels the low-volatility/betting-against-beta effect as the volatility risk premium; the rule as written still carries a real economic mechanism (leverage constraints and lottery demand behind the low-volatility spread), and country ETF prices are obtainable outside Bloomberg. Whether a market-neutral vol-sorted country book really delivers 1.5 net is for the statistics to settle.
queued.mechanism: The volatility risk premium implies that low-volatility assets earn a premium over high-volatility ones. A strategy that dynamically scales exposure to country equity ETFs based on their recent volatility can capture this premium. By applying it to a broad cross-section of countries, idiosyncratic risks are diversified.
queued.rule: At each month-end, compute the 20-day realized volatility for each country ETF. Sort the ETFs into quintiles based on this volatility. Go long the lowest-volatility quintile and short the highest-volatility quintile, with equal weight within each quintile. Hold for one month, then rebalance. The portfolio is market-neutral and volatility-diversified.
queued.title: Volatility-managed global equity factor ETFs
queued.why: at its claimed strength it expects t 5.196 against 3.0 (passes 99% of the time); the claim must be verified at its source before it is built
queued.why_new: The original volatility-managed country equity ETFs idea was dropped for lack of power (insufficient instruments). This version uses 30 country ETFs as one book, providing many more independent observations and thus sufficient power to reach the bar.

queued.critic_reason: The ETF NAV premium/discount family was dropped for lack of power ONLY, with the remedy stated as about nineteen years or about three independent instruments over the eight years as one book. Fifty ETFs traded as one book over eight years answers that lack, so this is a new test. Authorized-participant creation/redemption is a genuine microstructure mechanism, daily price and NAV history for a broad ETF cross-section is obtainable, and the signal is computed after the close and traded afterwards, so it can be run without look-ahead. The small size of typical premiums against the round trip, and the stale-NAV contamination for some ETF types, are matters of cost and measurement that the statistics must weigh, not grounds for rejection at this stage.
queued.data_source: Daily ETF price and NAV data from a data vendor
queued.mechanism: ETFs often deviate from their net asset value (NAV) due to supply-demand imbalances or short-term liquidity shocks. These deviations mean revert as authorized participants create or redeem shares to arbitrage the difference. Trading a large cross-section of ETFs diversifies the idiosyncratic risks of individual ETFs.
queued.rule: At the end of each trading day, compute the premium/discount for each ETF as (ETF price - NAV) / NAV. Rank the ETFs by this premium. Go long the quintile with the largest discounts (most negative premium) and short the quintile with the largest premiums (most positive), with equal weight. Hold for one trading day, then rebalance. Use a maximum of 10 longs and 10 shorts.
queued.title: ETF premium/discount mean reversion across many ETFs
queued.why: at its claimed strength it expects t 3.394 against 3.0 (passes 65% of the time); the claim must be verified at its source before it is built
queued.why_new: The original ETF NAV premium/discount mean reversion was dropped for lack of power on a small set of ETFs. This version uses a large cross-section of 50 ETFs as one book, greatly increasing the number of observations and thus statistical power.

today.critic_reason: The COT-based commodity hedging-pressure risk premium is distinct from COT-1's FX positioning test. It has an economic risk-premium mechanism, uses public CFTC and exchange data, and the Friday-release/Monday-open timing avoids look-ahead.
today.data_source: CFTC Commitments of Traders weekly reports (free) and CME daily settlement prices for 20 commodity futures.
today.evidence: de Roon, Nijman & Veld (2000, Journal of Finance) found hedging pressure predicts futures returns; Gorton, Hayashi & Rouwenhorst (2013, Review of Finance) linked commercial positioning and commodity risk premia.
today.mechanism: Commercial hedgers in commodity futures pay a risk premium to speculators for bearing price risk. When commercials are unusually net short, futures are cheap and subsequently earn positive returns; when they are unusually net long, the reverse. The pressure persists because hedgers are forced to transfer risk and speculators require compensation.
today.needs_short_or_leverage: Yes: it needs both long and short commodity-futures CFDs and leverage to hold the cross-sectional book.

ways: about 36 years of fresh data at the claimed strength, against the 9 it has
or the same mechanism on about 4 independent instruments over those 9 years, tested as one book

today.rule: Each Friday after the CFTC COT release (positions as of Tuesday), compute commercial net position divided by open interest for each of 20 commodity futures. On the next Monday open, go long the 5 futures with the most negative commercial net position (hedgers most short) and short the 5 with the most positive commercial net position (hedgers most long), equal weight. Exit at the following Monday open. The rule spans 20 instruments as one book.
today.title: Commodity futures hedging-pressure risk premium
today.why: even at its claimed strength it expects t 1.5 against a bar of 3.0: as it stands it cannot pass, so it is not built as it stands. It is kept with a plan: about 36 years of fresh data at the claimed strength, against the 9 it has; or the same mechanism on about 4 independent instruments over those 9 years, tested as one book
today.why_new: COT-1 tested CFTC positioning only as a directional signal for FX majors. This is a new market (a cross-section of 20 commodity futures) and a new mechanism (the hedging-pressure risk premium), not the energy term-structure premium already tested.

today.critic_reason: US high-yield OAS as a leading risk-appetite signal for EM FX is a plausible information-diffusion mechanism. FRED OAS data and EM FX daily data are obtainable, and no listed closed family exactly covers this signal.
today.data_source: FRED series BAMLH0A0HYM2 (ICE BofA US High Yield OAS) and daily EM FX spot rates from Bloomberg/Refinitiv.
today.mechanism: US high-yield credit spreads move first when global risk appetite changes. EM currencies are riskier and adjust with a lag because capital flows and investor attention are slow. Widening spreads predict EM FX weakness; tightening predicts strength. The delay persists because EM FX is less liquid and less closely watched than US credit.
today.needs_short_or_leverage: Yes: it needs short EM FX positions and leverage to run the long/short basket.

ways: about 36 years of fresh data at the claimed strength, against the 10 it has
or the same mechanism on about 4 independent instruments over those 10 years, tested as one book

today.rule: Each Friday close, compute the 5-day change in the ICE BofA US High Yield OAS. If the change is negative (spreads tightened), go long an equal-weight basket of 10 EM currencies against USD. If positive (spreads widened), go short the same basket. Hold one week and exit at the next Friday close. The rule spans 10 instruments as one book.
today.title: US high-yield credit spread diffusion into EM FX
today.why: even at its claimed strength it expects t 1.581 against a bar of 3.0: as it stands it cannot pass, so it is not built as it stands. It is kept with a plan: about 36 years of fresh data at the claimed strength, against the 10 it has; or the same mechanism on about 4 independent instruments over those 10 years, tested as one book
today.why_new: No test here has used US high-yield credit spreads as a leading signal for EM FX. em-fx-daily has zero tests, and the mechanism is information diffusion from credit markets, not the commodity-price or rate-differential channels already tested.

today.critic_reason: Cross-sectional short-term reversal in EM FX has a liquidity-provision mechanism. It is not the tested cross-sectional currency momentum family, and daily EM FX data can support a clean weekly cross-sectional test.
today.data_source: Daily EM FX spot rates from Bloomberg/Refinitiv or Yahoo Finance.
today.mechanism: Liquidity providers in EM FX absorb temporary order imbalances from large flows and central-bank operations. They require compensation, so currencies that have moved sharply over a few days partially reverse. The effect persists because EM FX liquidity is thin and order flow is not immediately offset.
today.needs_short_or_leverage: Yes: it needs both long and short EM FX positions and leverage to hold the cross-sectional book.

ways: about 36 years of fresh data at the claimed strength, against the 10 it has
or the same mechanism on about 4 independent instruments over those 10 years, tested as one book

today.rule: Each Friday close, rank 20 EM currencies by their 5-day return against USD. Go long the bottom quintile (4 currencies) and short the top quintile (4 currencies), equal weight. Hold one week and exit at the next Friday close. The rule spans 20 instruments as one book.
